blocks.x: ABSTRACT

Microbes perform a very important role in soil fertility and plant nutrition. Generally, people think that microbes are only agents of disease, but they perform several beneficial activities in soil fertility and mineral nutrition, hence the bio-geochemical cycle mediated by microbes such as nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, sulphur cycle, etc. Through the decomposition of organic matter, microbes recycle the nutrients in soil. Nitrogen fixation is occurring by microbes, either non-symbiotic or symbiotic. Rhizobium is the most common symbiotic bacteria, which can fix nitrogen biologically. Some of these bacteria, such as Micrococcus spp., Enterobacter aerogens, Pseudomonas capacia, and some fungi like Aspergillus niger, A. flavus, A. japonicas, and Penicillium sp., as well as actinomycetes like Streptomyces, can solubilize P and make it available to plants. Mycorrhiza helps the plant uptake nutrients from the deeper horizon, especially phosphorus. Mycorrhiza also mediated the non-toxification of some inorganic pollutants like As, Cd, Pb, and Cu. Compost and biofertilizer are made with the help of microbes to enhance soil fertility, which makes essential nutrients available to plants. These are also very eco-friendly and cost-effective. In the recent past, another important function of microbes has been invented, which is the role of microbes in storing atmospheric carbon is called carbon sequestration. Large-scale atmospheric carbon storage occurs in soil. Since carbon is the main reason for global warming, microbes play a great role by storing carbon in soil. Some ectomycorrhiza, Azolla, BGA, and bacteria can fix carbon. Carbon can persist in humus for a long time through the humification process.
Introduction

Microbes play an important role in soil health, food, agriculture production, industrial processes, and human health. One of the living resources in soil is the vast ocean of diverse microbes that ultimately support crop yield and soil health (Agrawal and Sharma, 2003). Living organisms, both plants and animals, constitute an important component of soil. Even though these organisms form only a fraction of the total soil mass, they play a major role in supporting plant communities on the earth’s surface. Soil life constitutes two types of organisms, namely macro-organisms and micro- organisms. Macro-organisms are those visible to the naked eye, and micro-organisms, or microbes, can be seen only with the help of a microscope.

The soil organisms are classified into two broad groups, viz., soil flora and soil fauna, which are again subdivided, depending upon their size, into soil macroflora and soil microflora, soil macrofauna and soil microfauna. Important groups in each class are shown in the following chart.

Decomposition of Organic Residues and Release of Plant Nutrients

The source of organic matter in soil is come from residues of plant, animals and soil microorganisms. Soil organic matter, the source of nutrients, is of complex nature that the crop plants can’t utilize it as such. Therefore, it is essential that this complex organic matter be decomposed into simple compound is performed by microorganisms particularly by bacteria and fungi. As a result, soil enriched with large amount of nutrients, which is available to plants. The organic materials (plant and animal residues) incorporated in the soil do not remain as such very long. A wide range of worms, insects, and microorganisms that are present in the soil, particularly if the soil is moist, attack them immediately. The microorganism for getting their food, break up the various constituents of which the organic residues are composed, and convert them into new different substances, some of which are very simple in composition and others highly complex. The whole of the organic residues is not decomposed all at once or as a whole. Some constituents are decomposed very quickly, whereas others are decomposed less readily and very slowly.

The process of conversion of proteins to amino acids is known as ammonization. (2) Breakdown of Cellulose- Cellulose is the most abundant carbohydrate found in plant waste. The microorganisms break up cellulose into cellobiose and glucose. Organisms continue to attack glucose and convert it into organic acids:

Acid soils decompose cellulose at a slower rate than neutral or alkaline soils. It is quite rapid in well-aerated soils but comparatively slow in poorly aerated soils. (3) Breakdown of Hemi-cellulose- When subjected to microbial decomposition, hemicelluloses is first hydrolysed to their component sugars and uronic acids. The sugars are further attacked by microorganisms. They are transformed into water, carbon dioxide, alcohols, and organic acids. Carbon dioxide and pentose are produced by the breakdown of uronic acids. The newly synthesised hemicelluloses thus form a part of the humus. Hemicelluloses decompose faster than cellulose. (4) Breakdown of Starch- Chemically, it is polymer of glucose. It is first hydrolysed into maltose by the action of enzymes (amylases). Maltose is next converted into glucose by another enzyme (maltase). Because glucose dissolves in water, it is used for metabolic processes such as growth. (C) Decomposition of Ether-soluble Substances- Fats are first broken down by micro-organisms through the agency of enzyme lipase into glycerol and fatty acids, Glycerol is then oxidized to organic acids, which, along with the other fatty acids, are ultimately oxidized to carbon dioxide and water. (D) Decomposition of Lignin- Lignin is deposited on the cell wall to strengthen the plant's skeletal framework. Lignin decomposes slowly, much slower than cellulose. It’s completely oxidizes to produce water and carbon dioxide.

Association of Plant Root and Fungus: On the roots of some plants or trees a few type of fungus grow and live symbiotically. This association of the fungi with the roots of higher plants is called Mycorrhiza that increases the surface area of absorption in plant roots. Mycorrhiza is very important in the uptake of nutrients such as P, N, K, Cu, Zn and Ca by plants especially in soil where these nutrients are present in low amount. P is the most limiting nutrient in tropical soils. Mycorrhiza is very important for improving P nutrition particularly for that soil. The thin mycorrhizal hyphae are able to penetrate soil pores not accessible to the root hairs which are about five times larger than the hyphae (Kirkby and Mengel, 2001). Studies have shown that the heavily mycorrhizal root of cassava enables it to grow well in phosphate deficient soils where other crops fail to grow (Wild, 1993). In alkaline soils, mycorrhizas have ability to prevent iron and manganese deficiencies. Carbon Sequesters- Mycorrhiza fungi are associated with plant roots and gets sugar from root exudation. They use sugar and help plants to uptake more water and nutrients. By eating sugars Mycorrhiza fungi deposits carbon containing residues in surrounding soil. Ectomyccorhiza fungi help to storing 50%- 70% carbon in soil (Averill, et al. 2014) Sequester Bacteria There are some aerobic bacteria such as Knallgas bacteria (Chemo-lithoautotrophs). As a carbon source some anaerobic bacteria and archaea (e.g., acetogenic bacteria, carbon moxideutilizer, methanogenogens) use carbon dioxide and can fix C.

Microbial Induced Nutrient Deficiency: When organic matter of high C: N ratio or less nitrogen content like rice straw is added to the soil, there is a profound increase in the microbial population of soil in order to decompose the organic matter. Since the plant residue is deficient in nitrogen, microbial nitrogen requirement is fulfilled from the available native nitrogen content of the soil. This creates temporary deficiency symptoms are visually observed on the plants. However, this deficiency Al2O3K2O6SiO2 + 4H2SO4 Bacillus siliceous Al2(SO4)3 +K2SO4 + 6SiO2+ 4H2O is short lived and is recovered when the locked up nitrogen in microbial tissues is autolysed and released in the soil. Therefore, undecomposed plant material with high C:N ratio or less nitrogen content should not be added to the soil at the time of sowing or during plant growth. Biological Nitrogen Fixation: Nitrogen is an important macro essential element for plants. It is in atmosphere up to 78% of the total atmospheric gases in the form of gaseous or elemental nitrogen. But it can’t be utilized by crop plants, unless this gaseous form of nitrogen is converted into combined form of nitrogen namely ammonium. There are a number of useful microorganisms that have capacity to convert the atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium. So, the process of conversion of molecular nitrogen into complex proteins through the agency of biological organisms is known as biological nitrogen fixation. Such nitrogen fixation, particularly, the symbiotic one, is of great economic importance in crop production and the legumes have a place of prominence in crop rotations (Singh, 2003). Nitrogen fixing microorganisms can be divided broadly into two groups: (1) Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixers- This group of bacteria which, in association with the root nodules of leguminous plants, fix molecular nitrogen from air is grouped under the genus Rhizobium. They reduce atmospheric nitrogen and make it available to plants. The plants, in turn, provide carbohydrates for the nutrition of the bacteria. This association in which both the partners derive mutual benefit is known as symbiosis. This type conversion of molecular nitrogen to its reduced form is known as symbiotic nitrogen fixation. It is now known that a few non legumes are also capable of symbiotic nitrogen fixation.

This group of nitrogen fixing bacteria in soil is heterotrophic aerobic microorganisms occur in the root region of legumes and non legumes. Rhizobium is preferentially stimulated in the rhizosphere of legumes than in that of non legumes.

(2) Non symbiotic nitrogen fixers- Certain free living bacteria have the ability to fix molecular nitrogen from air. To this group belong Azotobacter, Clostridium, Azospirillum, Azolla and Beijerinckia. Besides bacteria, algae also fix atmospheric nitrogen. Bacteria which can fix nitrogen independently without association with any other organism are called non symbiotic nitrogen fixing bacteria and the process is non symbiotic nitrogen fixation.

Reclamation of Saline-Alkaline Soils: Useful role of some microorganisms in the improvement of saline alkaline soils have been reported growing Blue green algae in saline alkaline soil for a larger period improves the soil properties. This is because of the preferential absorption or adsorption of sodium by them. The growth of these Blue green algae in saline alkaline habitat reduces salinity by 25-30%, pH, EC and exchangeable sodium.
Evaluation of Soil Fertility status: Some microorganisms Azotobactor, Aspergillus, Cumminghmela etc. have been employed to evaluate the soil fertility status particularly for Phosphorus and Potassium
Factors affecting microbial activity

Soil organisms are in constant competition for organically bound carbon and other nutrients. Their ability to get these growth materials depends on temperature, moisture, soil reaction (acidity or alkalinity), nutrient regimes of soil, appropriate source of energy and competition with the microorganisms etc. Since the soil organisms are of divergent nature, it is not possible to define the same favourable conditions for all microorganisms due to different optima exists in different groups of soil organisms. However, some general conditions affecting activities of soil organisms are briefly described below:

(i) Moisture- Dryness kills many microbes and many microorganisms develop resistant strains or enter a dormant stage. Microorganisms are less active at the wilting percentage for plants (less water for their mobility) or at the other extreme saturated soil (very poor action) conditions. Anaerobes, comprising a very small portion of soil microbes, grow best at saturated waterlogged soil conditions. However, majority of soil microorganisms are most active at field capacity soil moisture level. (ii) Soil reaction- The majority of soil organisms especially microorganisms grow best at neutral soil reaction (pH 7.0) which is the pH of microbial cytoplasm (the cell material). Bacteria and actinomycetes are generally less tolerant of acidic soil reactions than fungi, which can grow in a range of soil conditions. An exception is the sulphur oxidising genus Thiobacillus (produces H2SO4) that tolerates soil pH even as low as pH 0.6. Localized microenvironments near roots or decomposing wastes can result in lower soil pH than the overall system.

(iii) Aeration- Microbes consume oxygen from soil air and give out carbon dioxide. Oxygen in soil is renewed through the process of diffusion and mass flow of atmospheric air. In the absence of such gaseous exchange, carbon dioxide accumulates in soil air and becomes toxic to the microbes. Rate of oxygen intake and simultaneous evolution of carbon dioxide are measures of microbial activity. (iv) Light- Direct sunlight is injurious to most of the microorganisms except algae. (v) Temperature- The activity of most of soil organisms accelerates with the rise in soil temperature. There are exceptions that can exist fairly well at very cold temperatures (psychrophiles cold lovers) and others exist at high temperatures (thermophiles heat lovers). But the majority of soil bacteria and actinomycetes show optimum activity at temperatures similar to those of the mesophiles (middle group organisms).

There are generally three groups based on temperatures as follows: Psychrophiles. Grow at temperatures <5°C (< 41°F), but have optimum temperatures near that of mesophiles. Mesophiles. Grow slightly near 0°C (32°F). Optimum temperatures are usually between 25°C and 37°C (77- 90°F). Thermophiles. This group of organisms can tolerate 45- 75°C (113-167°F) with optima between 55 and 65°C (131-149°F).

(vi) Nutrients- Micro-organisms have greater demands for nutrients for their growth and development, especially for N, P, S. and Ca, so the optimum amount of those nutrients should be present in the soil. Organisms compete for nutrients with other species of organisms and even with each other.

(vii) Organic matter- Soil having moderate to high organic matter are most favourable for the optimum growth and development of most of the soil organisms especially for the bacteria that live on the soil organic matter and become active.

(viii) Microbial products- Some soil antibodies substances that retard or kill other beneficial microorganisms in the soil. Besides, the competition for nutrients among different microbes can also be eliminated and thereby a particular group of microorganisms gains more nutrients and consequently increases its activity.

(ix) Microbial association- Microorganisms interact with one another giving rise to antagonistic or symbiotic relations. The association existing between one organism and another whether of symbiotic or antagonistic nature influences the activities of the soil population to a certain extent. Many organisms act as predators and parasites. Sometimes they kill many of beneficial soil microorganisms in soil and indirectly inhibit many important transformations like mineral nutrients transformation, decomposition of organic matter, fixation of nitrogen (gain of N) in soil etc. which affect plant growth and development.
Bacteriophages are viruses that parasitize bacteria, causing death and partial breakdown.
Challenges Faced in Exploiting Soil Microorganisms

There are a number of factors that derail maximization of beneficial microbial activities. Apart from climatic factors, there are a number of anthropogenic or social factors that affect biological functions and soil productivity. Chianu, et al. (2012) noted the following some of the main challenges faced in exploiting beneficial activities of soil microorganisms for improving soil fertility and productivity:
(i) Absence or very weak institutions, policy and budgetary support for research. (ii) Limited knowledge of inoculation.
(iii) Poorly developed marketing channels and infrastructure and limited involvement of the private sector in the distribution of inoculants.
(iv) Limited farmer awareness about and access to inoculants.
(v) Lack of development of technology in this field.
CONCLUSIONS

From this review it is noted that soil microorganisms have a huge contribution in soil fertility. This is achieved through a number of ways. Biological nitrogen fixation is an economically attractive and ecologically sound route for augmenting nutrient supply. The widely known Rhizobium/legume symbiosis improves crops that come after in rotation and supplies large amounts of biologically fixed nitrogen to cropping systems. Soil microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi contribute to plant phosphorus nutrition through solubilisation of fixed or precipitated phosphorus from complexes with Al and Fe in acidic soils and calcium complexes in alkaline soils. Phosphate solubilising rhizospheric bacteria has a high potential to be used in the management of P deficient soils. Mycorrhizal associations are reported to contribute to plant phosphorus nutrition through increasing root surface area for soil exploration, production of phosphorus solubilising, enzymes and organic acids. Mycorrhiza fungi and bacteria also solubilise other nutrients such as zinc, copper, and calcium. Microorganisms also contribute to soil fertility improvements through their roles in composting. Soil microorganisms are currently isolated, studied and packaged as biofertilizer and used to supplement chemical fertilizers. As chemical-based fertilizers (nitrogenous fertilizers) harm the environment, but the importance of biofertilizer is growing significantly. In contrast, biofertilizer lead to soil enrichment and are compatible with long term sustainability. They are not harmful to the environment and are eco-friendly as well. Again, SOC is a vital component of soil and have important on terrestrial ecosystem. From interaction among the dynamic ecological processes of photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition which mediated by microbes, net carbon are store in soil. Carbon dioxide is increased greatly by human activities, but now human activities provide an opportunity for sequestering carbon back into soil. Carbon sequestration also improve soil quality by maintaining and increasing soil organic matter adds to soil fertility, water retention and crop production. It can be noted that thorough exploitation of microbial activities can contribute to balanced fertilization and carbon storage for long term which help in improving long term soil health.
